human_tolerance.notes: No terrestrial wild population lives near people: the species is tied to Antarctic fast ice and is protected by the Antarctic Treaty and the Convention for the Conservation of Antarctic Seals. The one recurring human presence is research, and the animals tolerate it closely - their fast-ice habitat is often adjacent to Antarctic bases, which is why their life history is so well documented.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Spring birthing on the fast ice. Depending on latitude a female gives birth between early September and November, those at lower latitudes dropping their pup earliest; one pup is born in one to four minutes, occasionally twins. Pups weigh 25-30 kg (about half their mother's length), double that in their first week, take their first swim at one to two weeks, and are weaned and hunting independently after six to seven weeks.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: Austral-spring mating, from late November to December, once pups are weaned and females begin ovulating. Males hold and defend underwater territories on the fast-ice breathing holes and fight rivals. Copulation is underwater; the female is then bitten on the neck if she tries to leave. Fertilised eggs wait out the winter: the embryo does not implant until mid-January to mid-February, so birth always falls in the following spring's window.

phases.name: moult
phases.note: The annual moult of the thin fur coat, around the beginning of austral summer. Coats may change to shades of brown before it; pups, born with a grey lanugo, moult at three to four weeks and then darken towards the adult colour.

vocalizations.description: A repetitive sequence of the same vocal elements, varying only slightly over time, with every individual keeping its own song; singing is uncommon. During the austral-spring mating season the calls carry far enough to be felt through the ice.
The high, urgent call a hungry pup gives to alert its mother, and the call mothers use to summon a pup from a distance once scent can no longer be used efficiently to find it.

external.note: GBIF usage key 2434784 and ITIS TSN 180669 from their own records; Wikidata Q313166 for the item, and NCBI taxon id 9713 from its P685 claim.

common_names.note: English, French and German labels from Wikidata (en "Weddell seal", fr "Phoque de Weddell", de "Weddellrobbe").

conservation.note: Wikipedia's conservation section: "It is classified as being of 'least concern' by the IUCN"; Wikidata's P141 for Q313166 is Q211005 (least concern). IUCN Red List pages themselves are not openly licensed, so neither is cited.

range.note: "a relatively large and abundant true seal with a circumpolar distribution surrounding Antarctica"; "primarily restricted to Antarctic waters"; the species occupies fast ice off the Antarctic continent, so AQ is the whole native range. The one population outside the continent, in South Georgia, is a South Atlantic island and not a separate ISO 3166-1 country.

traits.limb_count.note: "They have streamlined bodies and four limbs that are modified into flippers."

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Swim: phocids "primarily use their hind limbs" to propel themselves in the water, and the Weddell seal is a phocid. Walk: phocid "terrestrial locomotion ... is more cumbersome" than an otariid's, but the Weddell seal does move over the ice - it "gather[s] in small groups around cracks and holes within the ice" and moves regionally to follow the breathing holes as the ice changes. No open source gives a running or bounding gait, so only Walk and Swim are listed.

traits.thermoregulation.note: A mammal (GBIF class Mammalia) whose pups warm themselves by shivering: the article's thermoregulation section reports high muscle enzyme activity in newborn Weddell seals, "a primary thermoregulatory strategy of these seals includes muscle thermogenesis, or shivering".

traits.skin.note: "The Weddell seal grows a thin fur coat around its whole body except for small areas around the flippers."

traits.flight.note: A pinniped is flightless: all four limbs are flippers and none is a wing. The schema requires this field, so it is stated explicitly as None rather than left out.

traits.respiration.note: Breathes air at holes it maintains in the fast ice; in winter it stays in the water "with only their heads poking through breathing holes in the ice".

traits.nest_type.note: Nothing is built: a pup is born directly on the fast ice ("Weddell seals return to fast ice colonies during the spring for birthing and breeding"), and in winter the adults shelter in the water rather than in any den. Hence None, not Ground.

traits.senses.note: Olfaction High: during a pup's first two weeks "mother Weddell seals distinguish their pups through scent", and mothers stop relying on scent when they have to call a pup from a distance. The schema's other senses fields are left out: the article describes reliance on eyesight in daylight and on the vibrissae in darkness, but it states no colour vision, no night vision, no hearing level and no ultraviolet use.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (400 kg, well above the Medium bound of 50 kg).

traits.mass_kg.note: EltonTraits MamFuncDat BodyMass-Value 400000 g (BodyMass-SpecLevel 1, species-level; source Ref_117, Smith et al. 2003). It sits at the bottom of Wikipedia's "400-600 kg" range, which also notes males "usually about 500 kg or less".

traits.mass_range_kg.note: "weigh 400-600 kg (880-1,320 lb)", used as the adult range as given.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of "Weddell seals measure about 2.5-3.5 m (8 ft 2 in - 11 ft 6 in) long", taken as the typical adult length; males and females "are generally about the same length".

traits.speed_ms.note: Swim only, and only for pinnipeds as a group: "typically swimming at 5-15 kn (9-28 km/h)". The midpoint (10 kn) converts to 5.1 m/s and is used as the typical swim speed. No open source gives a Weddell seal swimming speed, and none gives any land speed, so no walk speed is set and the importer falls back to the body-plan default.

traits.lifespan_y.note: The only figure any open source gives: "The maximum lifespan of the species is estimated at least 25 years." No mean or typical longevity is published, so this is a documented ceiling entered in a field the schema describes as a typical lifespan.

traits.diet.note: EltonTraits MamFuncDat for Leptonychotes weddellii: Diet-Vfish 60, Diet-Inv 40, Diet-Vend 0, Diet-Vect 0, Diet-Scav 0, Diet-Certainty ABC (source Ref_98, Stirling 1971). The 60/40 split needs no mapping into the schema's vocabulary: fish is a schema diet key and the invertebrate share is cephalopods and crustaceans. Wikipedia agrees on the shape - "Antarctic cod and Antarctic silverfish constitute the majority of their diet. Cephalopods are common prey, and crustacean remains are sometimes found in Weddell seal scat, but at much lower rates than other prey species." No non-fish vertebrate share is recorded: the article reports attacks on four penguin species but "it has not been confirmed ... if the penguins were consumed", so vertebrate is left at 0.

traits.social.note: Colony: seals "gather in small groups around cracks and holes within the ice", and "fast ice breeding grounds cause females to cluster in large aggregations". The group_size bracket is authored, not measured - no open source counts a Weddell seal group; 1 is a single animal at one breathing hole and 100 stands for the "large aggregations" of a breeding ground.

traits.activity_pattern.note: EltonTraits MamFuncDat Activity-Diurnal 1, Activity-Nocturnal 0, Activity-Crepuscular 0. Wikipedia agrees in substance: "These seals exhibit a diel dive pattern, diving deeper and longer during the day than at night."

traits.defense.note: Flee: at sea the species is prey to killer whales and leopard seals, "which prey primarily on juveniles and pups", and a disturbed animal on the ice makes for the water. The schema has no value for the teeth-baring threat display of territorial males, and "no natural predators when on fast ice" describes exposure rather than a response.

traits.wariness.note: Authored judgement, low. "They have no natural predators when on fast ice", and the fast-ice habitat this species occupies is "often adjacent to Antarctic bases", so animals sit among people and research teams without bolting; they are not indifferent to being handled or to an orca, hence not 0.

habitat.use.note: EltonTraits ForStrat-Value "M" = marine (the dataset's own key: "M - marine, G - ground level, including aquatic foraging, S - scansorial, Ar - arboreal, A - aerial"). Every stratum share is therefore aquatic.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: water: "In the winter, they stay in the water to avoid blizzards, with only their heads poking through breathing holes in the ice." Outside the winter the animal rests hauled out on the ice, for which the schema has no tag.

habitat.resources.note: Predation weights are the EltonTraits diet shares. The schema's tag list has no `fish` tag, so the 0.6 fish share is carried by `small_vertebrate` - the fish this species eats (Antarctic cod and silverfish) are small vertebrates - and the 0.4 cephalopod-and-crustacean share by `invertebrate`; `traits.diet` keeps the distinction explicit. The `water` entry is the animal's total dependence on a hole and the water under it.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Avoider, and never a garden or suburb animal: the range is Antarctic fast ice, the species "is protected by the Antarctic Treaty and the Convention for the Conservation of Antarctic Seals", and "its life history ... is well documented since it occupies fast ice environments close to the Antarctic continent and often adjacent to Antarctic bases". No distance, impervious, light or noise tolerance is set, because no open source gives one for an animal that never meets built land.

seasonal.strategy.note: "Weddell seals are non-migratory phocids ... that move regionally to follow the distribution of breathing holes and exit cracks within the ice changes between seasons" - resident all year, so ActiveYearRound with no dormancy triggers.

seasonal.phases.note: Windows authored from the dates in the breeding and moult text, on the southern calendar. Young: "this marine mammal gives birth from early September through November, with those living at lower latitudes giving birth earlier", weaning "after six to seven weeks". Mating: "The mating season occurs during austral spring between late November and December after pups are weaned and females begin ovulating", with males holding and defending territories. Moult: "This coat moults around the beginning of summer"; the austral summer, hence a window that wraps over New Year. No `region` is given: the whole range is one population and the timing shifts only with latitude, which the phases' notes carry.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Duration 45 days is the midpoint of the stated weaning age, "after six to seven weeks", which is also when pups "begin to hunt independently". Scale 0.5 is the stated birth size, "The pups are around half the length of their mother at birth" (25-30 kg against an adult 400-600 kg, rising to about 100 kg at weaning); a single scale cannot express that growth, so the birth figure is used.

vocalizations.song.note: "There have been recordings of Weddell seal vocalisations that are described as songs. Their songs consist of repetitive sequences of the same vocal elements, and they only vary slightly over time. Individual Weddell seals can each produce their unique song, but singing behaviour is not common." Loudness is taken from "During the mating season, Weddell seals make noises loud enough to be felt through the ice", which is why the months are the Nov-Dec mating window even though the song description states no season. The article also records that "Weddell seals commonly produce ultrasonic vocalizations" whose "functional significance is yet unknown"; that is deliberately not given its own entry, because the schema requires a context and the record has no basis for one. No frequency band or duration is given because no open source states either, and no recording is linked because no openly licensed recording of this species was verifiable.

vocalizations.pup_call.note: "Pups also use higher, more urgent vocalisations when hungry to alert their mothers to feed", and "Mother Weddell seals use vocalisations to call their pups from further distances when smell can no longer be used efficiently". Months follow the September-November birthing window in which a mother and pup pair up. Cooldown and loudness are authored.

look.note: Colours judged from the described coat: adults are "counter-shaded ... from bluish-black to dark grey dorsally and to light grey/silver ventrally", coats "may change to shades of brown before the annual moult", and the fur is absent "around the flippers", so `body` is the dark bluish-grey back, `belly` the silver-grey underside, and `markings` the dark brown-black of the bare flipper skin, which the `leg_*` parts are coloured with. A box carries one colour, so the silver ventral surface only shows on the `snout` part, which the body plan already paints from `belly`. Proportions are authored for a seal built as a `quadruped`: torso_aspect 2.5 and girth_ratio 1.3 for the "bulky body", leg_length_ratio 0.1 so the four flippers come out as low stubby boxes, head_scale 0.65 and beak_ratio 0.25 for a small blunt muzzle, neck_angle_deg 0 to carry the head level with the back rather than raised, tail_ratio 0.05 for the small tail, and ear_ratio 0 because phocids "lack" external ears. The `shoulder` extra part is the one non-obvious piece: the quadruped builder hard-codes a neck 32% of torso length, which on a 3 m animal left a 0.4 m bar of empty space between body and head and read as a fox rather than a seal, so a full-height block flush with the body closes that gap and the head grows straight out of it; its size was set in the previewer, not from a measurement. `shoulder_height_m` is deliberately left out: a seal has no standing posture and no open source gives one, and in the mesh builder a shoulder height overrides leg_length_ratio outright, which would undo the flipper proportions above.

behavior.note: Authored. The three shared programs do not fit: fsm-ground-forager-v1 forages on the surface, drinks from open water and rests in a shelter, fsm-anuran-nocturnal-v1 hides in cover by day and hops away from threats, and bt-perching-songbird-v1 perches and flies - none of them has a haul-out/dive cycle, which is the whole year-round behaviour of a phocid. The bespoke fsm-pinniped-haulout-v1 rests hauled out, dives to feed with the swim gait, sings through the austral-spring mating months, and slides away from a threat; food_m 400, flee_m 15 and calm_m 40 are judgement, chosen for an animal that covers long distances underwater but is slow and awkward on ice. dive_depth_m 600 is the deepest observed dive and haul_out_hours 8 the haul-out dwell; both reach the machine through the schema's blackboard predicate, because this format's duration fields are in seconds and no predicate takes a length in metres, and the machine still cycles on hunger if the host publishes neither.
